#### [The Spark]{.smallcaps}

[Makeover Monday's Week 47 challenge](https://makeovermonday.vercel.app/dataset/what-does-likely-actually-mean)
featured a 19 × 19 heatmap from the
[CAPphrase project](https://adamkucharski.github.io/CAPphrase/). Each cell shows how often respondents judged one probability phrase
higher than another. Cells near 50/50 are colored red, and the legend calls
them "most inconsistent."

I had explored this dataset earlier, in TidyTuesday Week 10
([Lost in the Middle](https://stevenponce.netlify.app/data_visualizations/TidyTuesday/2026/tt_2026_10.html)),
looking at the numeric estimates people give each phrase. This time the
label raised a different question: inconsistent at what level, the crowd or
the individual? A 50/50 cell says the crowd split. It doesn't say that any
one person wavered.

#### [The Detour]{.smallcaps}

The data held a way to test that. Each of 5,174 respondents made ten
comparisons, and comparison 10 repeated comparison 1 with the two phrases on
swapped sides. The original chart's 342 cells reproduce exactly only when
those repeated answers are included.

That repeat separates two questions:

- **Between people:** how often do two different respondents answer the same
  pair differently?
- **Within a person:** how often does one respondent change their own answer?

The heatmap shows how the crowd answered. Its label suggests something about
how individuals behave. Those are two different questions, and only the
repeat can speak to the second.

I limited the test to the 18 pairs that divided the crowd, where
the more popular answer accounted for 50 to 70% of first responses. That
left 612 respondents who saw one of those pairs twice.

#### [The Check]{.smallcaps}

The within-person rate is observed: the share of those 612 whose second
answer differed from their first. The between-person rate has to be
estimated. If a share *p* of respondents pick one phrase, two independently
drawn responses disagree with probability 2*p*(1 − *p*).

Two decisions mattered.

First, the benchmark could not reuse the answers it was meant to evaluate.
My first calculation drew *p* from answers that included comparison 1, the
first half of the repeated question. I corrected that by estimating *p* from
comparisons 2 to 9 only. The correction kept the answers used to estimate
crowd disagreement separate from those used to measure individual reversals.

Second, the selection rule constrained the benchmark before any result
arrived:

```r
between <- function(p) 2 * p * (1 - p)
between(c(0.50, 0.60, 0.70))

# 0.50 0.48 0.42   <- pairs split 50-70% can only land between 42% and 50%
```

The benchmark was always going to be close to 50%. Its exact value, 46.5%,
comes from the data. It is a yardstick, not an independently observed
disagreement rate.

#### [The Chart]{.smallcaps}

![Two horizontal bars on a shared 0 to 100% track, titled "A divided crowd
doesn't mean most people change their answers." When the same person was
asked a divided phrase pair again a few questions later, their two answers
differed 12.3% of the time (burgundy bar; 95% bootstrap interval 7.6% to
15.5%; 612 people re-asked). For two different people, each answering once,
the estimated probability of differing answers was 46.5% (stone bar; 95% bootstrap interval
45.1% to 48.1%). A note explains that this rate sits near 50% by design,
because the pairs were chosen to split the crowd.](/data_visualizations/MakeoverMonday/2026/mm_2026_47.png){#fig-1}

Asked the same pair again, 12.3% of the 612 changed their answer, against a
46.5% benchmark for two different people.

The first version of this chart failed my own comprehension review. I read
the two bars as two groups of people, the percentages had no stated
meaning, and the intervals had no labels. The final version names two
answering situations instead, "two different people, each answering once"
and "the same person, asked again a few questions later," and says what
each interval is.

The limits stay in view. The repeat came nine comparisons later in the same
sitting, so memory may have held the change rate down. The sides were always
swapped, with an unknown effect. Most respondents kept their original answer
within this short quiz. That says nothing about whether answers would hold
over weeks, or about why people disagree.

#### [The Takeaway]{.smallcaps}

**A statistic can be computed correctly and still be given the wrong
meaning. Before attaching a word like "inconsistent" to a number, check that
the unit of analysis can support it.**

A split crowd describes the group. Individual inconsistency requires
evidence from the same person. This dataset happened to contain the repeat
that could supply it. Most datasets don't, and then the honest move is to
describe the split and stop there.
